passage: Few political promises are as widely shared as the promise of social mobility. Parties that agree on little else agree that a child's prospects should not be fixed by the circumstances of her birth, and the claim that mobility has stalled is one of the most damaging charges that can be laid against a government. Yet the word covers two quite different things, and much public argument about it goes astray because the two are run together.

The first is absolute mobility: the share of people who end up better off than their parents, whether by income or by the kind of work they do. The second is relative mobility: the extent to which a person's position in the distribution, as opposed to their standard of living, differs from their parents' position. The two can move independently. In a period of rapid growth and expanding professional employment, most children may outearn their parents and many may enter occupations their parents never held, even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top, compared with that of a child born near the top, has not changed at all. Everyone rides the escalator up, but the order of people on it stays the same.

This distinction explains a puzzle. When growth slows and the expansion of professional jobs levels off, absolute mobility falls, and people who do no better than their parents feel, reasonably enough, that something has closed. They often conclude that society has become less fair. Imagine a town where a mill employed one generation and new offices employed the next. The children did better than their parents without anyone being pushed aside, and the town experienced this as openness. When the offices stop hiring, the grandchildren find that the climb has ended, though their chances against the children of the office managers may be exactly what their parents' chances were. But on the measures that track relative position, the chances may be much as they were: what has disappeared is not openness but the rising tide that once let a whole generation move up without anyone having to move down. The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken.

The distinction also exposes an awkwardness that politicians prefer to leave unspoken. Absolute mobility can, in principle, be enjoyed by everyone at once. Relative mobility cannot. If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall, and a serious commitment to relative mobility is therefore a commitment to downward mobility for some children of the comfortable. It is not surprising that the comfortable resist it, often without any sense of doing so, through the ordinary devices of private tuition, a well-placed word, or the purchase of a house near the right school. Each of these looks like ordinary care for one's own children; together they amount to a defence of position.

None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one. Absolute mobility answers a question about material progress: are people living better than their parents did? Relative mobility answers a question about fairness: does birth still decide where one ends up? Both questions matter, and neither is easy to answer with confidence, since incomes fluctuate and occupations change their meaning across generations. But a society that wants more of the second kind should be honest that it cannot be had at no one's expense, and a society that mourns the loss of the first should not mistake a slower economy for a more rigid one.

passage: We tend to read the history of life as a long tournament in which the better designed win. On this view a lineage that disappeared must have had some flaw, and the dinosaurs, the textbook losers, are pictured as sluggish and outmoded long before their end. The picture is comfortable because it makes the present inhabitants of the earth look like deserving champions. For the most dramatic episodes in the record it is also misleading. During ordinary stretches of geological time, extinction does seem to track the qualities that adaptation produces: species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift, and their places are taken by competitors that cope better. The great mass extinctions, in which a large fraction of species disappeared within a geologically brief interval, seem to follow different rules.

Consider the end of the Cretaceous period, when an asteroid struck the earth and the non-avian dinosaurs vanished along with many other groups. What determined survival in the aftermath was not, as far as can be told, excellence at the ways of life that had served well for millions of years. It was the possession of traits that happened to matter in a sudden catastrophe: small body size, a varied diet, the ability to shelter or to wait out a period of darkness and scarcity in a dormant state. Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced. They were, from the point of view of the crisis, accidents.

The consequence is that mass extinctions can redirect the history of life in ways that ordinary selection would not. A group that had been flourishing, and that would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions, can be swept away, while a group that had been marginal for tens of millions of years inherits an emptied world. The mammals, which had lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs for a very long time, are the familiar example. Their later success says little about whether they were superior to the non-avian dinosaurs in any absolute sense; it says that they passed through a narrow gate that the dinosaurs, for reasons unrelated to their earlier success, did not.

This does not mean that mass extinctions are pure lotteries. Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things. Nor does it mean that adaptation is unimportant, since the survivors went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed. What it does mean is that the long-run shape of life's history cannot be read as a straightforward measure of design quality. To understand why some groups are here and others are not, we need to know not only how well they fitted their world but also which rare disasters that world happened to contain.

passage: Few rules of modern etiquette are enforced as fiercely as the ban on spoilers. A friend who reveals the ending of a film that you have not yet seen is treated as though he had stolen something from you, and online discussions of new releases now arrive wrapped in warnings. Behind the etiquette lies a theory about what stories are for. On this view, the value of a narrative is concentrated in the not-knowing, and once the outcome is known the thing is used up, like a lottery ticket that has already been scratched.

The theory is difficult to square with how people actually behave. Children demand the same bedtime story night after night and object loudly if a single word is changed. Adults rewatch favourite films until they can recite the dialogue, and they reread novels whose endings they could describe in a sentence. Audiences at tragedies drawn from well-known legends have always known that the hero will die; for centuries this knowledge did not stop them from attending, and it may even have been part of the attraction. If knowing the ending destroyed the pleasure, none of this would make sense.

What these cases suggest is that suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome. A viewer can know perfectly well that the hero survives and still grip the arm of the chair when the rope begins to fray, because attention is absorbed in the unfolding moment rather than in a calculation about the final scene. Much of what we enjoy in a story, moreover, lies in the manner of its telling: the rhythm of a scene, the turn of a phrase, the way a minor character reveals himself in a single gesture. None of this is spoiled by a summary of the plot, since a summary is precisely what leaves it out.

It would be too much to conclude that spoilers do no harm at all. Some stories are built around a single reversal, and the shock of the first encounter with it is a real pleasure that cannot be had twice; a mystery whose solution has been announced in advance loses something that rereading does not restore. The etiquette, then, protects something genuine. But what it protects is a narrow and unrepeatable pleasure, not the whole value of a story, and a culture that treats the ending as the only thing worth guarding may gradually forget how to enjoy everything that comes before it.

passage: Few images of empire are as familiar as that of European diplomats bent over a map of Africa, ruler in hand, dividing a continent they had barely visited. The image is usually summoned to explain why so many of the continent's borders run in straight lines, and why so many of its states have struggled: the borders, it is said, were artificial, cutting across peoples and lumping together others who had nothing in common, and the conflicts of the post-colonial era are their bitter harvest. The story has the merit of placing responsibility where much of it belongs. As an explanation, however, it is weaker than its popularity suggests.

Begin with the image itself. The conference held in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 is often remembered as the moment of partition, but it chiefly agreed on rules by which European powers would recognise one another's claims. Most actual boundaries were settled afterwards, over decades, through bilateral treaties, exchanges of territory and survey commissions, and many of them followed rivers, watersheds or the limits of existing polities rather than lines of latitude. The straight lines are real, but they cluster in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.

More fundamentally, the charge of artificiality proves too much. Every border is artificial in the sense that people drew it, and many of the borders of Europe were fixed by wars, dynastic marriages and peace conferences no more attentive to local wishes than any colonial commission. If artificial borders caused instability by themselves, much of the world would be permanently at war. Nor is it obvious what a natural border would be. Peoples overlap, migrate and intermarry; a line that united one group would divide another. When African states gained independence, their leaders, aware of these difficulties, chose through the Organisation of African Unity to accept the boundaries they had inherited rather than reopen them, judging that an attempt to redraw them would be more dangerous than living with them.

None of this acquits the colonial powers. Boundaries were indeed drawn without consulting the people they affected, and some did separate communities from their pastures, markets and kin. But the more serious legacy lay inside the lines rather than in their placement: states built for extraction, with administrations designed to collect revenue and keep order rather than to represent, and with ethnic categories hardened by colonial policy into the main currency of politics. To blame the shape of the map is to look at the frame and miss the picture.

passage: An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries.

This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want.

The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance.

Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop.

passage: The model of the national park that spread across much of the world in the twentieth century rested on a simple picture: nature is most fully itself where people are absent, and the task of conservation is to keep them out. Boundaries were drawn, guards were posted, and in many places the people who had lived within the new boundaries, herding, gathering, farming small plots or hunting, were moved elsewhere. Critics have come to call this approach fortress conservation, and the name captures both its method and its mood.

The picture of untouched nature was often historically false. Many landscapes that visitors admired as wilderness had been shaped for centuries by the people who were then removed: grasslands kept open by grazing and deliberate burning, forests whose composition reflected generations of selective harvesting and planting. Removing those people did not return the land to an original state; it began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline. The costs to the displaced were, of course, more direct: the loss of homes, of access to food and medicine, of graves and sacred places, often with little or no compensation.

It would be too simple, however, to conclude that local residents are always the best stewards and that exclusion is never justified. Communities change, markets reach into forests, and a population that once harvested lightly may, under new pressures, begin to clear or hunt at rates the land cannot sustain. Some species, particularly those that are very sensitive to disturbance, may genuinely need areas where human presence is kept to a minimum. The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading as the image of untouched wilderness that it seeks to replace.

What the critique of fortress conservation establishes, then, is not a rule but a burden of proof. Exclusion imposes certain and heavy costs on identifiable people, while its benefits to wildlife are often assumed rather than shown. Where those who would be displaced have a long record of use compatible with the values being protected, the presumption should lie with their remaining, and with arrangements that give them a real share in managing the land. Where that record is absent, or where a species' needs are demonstrably incompatible with human use, exclusion may be defended; but it must be defended, case by case, rather than taken as the natural form of protection.

passage: In many parts of the world, groups of neighbours, co-workers or traders meet at regular intervals and each contributes a fixed sum to a common pot, which is then handed in its entirety to one member. At the next meeting the process is repeated and the pot goes to someone else, until every member has received it once and the cycle ends or begins again. The order may be fixed by lot, by agreement or, in some versions, by bidding, with the member who most urgently wants the money accepting a smaller pot and the difference shared among the rest. Such rotating associations go by dozens of local names, and for a long time development economists regarded them as makeshift substitutes for banks, ingenious but destined to disappear once formal credit reached the people who used them.

That prediction has fared poorly. The associations persist among people who have bank accounts, and they have travelled with migrants into cities where banks are on every corner. Their persistence is puzzling on a narrow financial view. For those who receive the pot early, the arrangement is an interest-free loan; for those who receive it late, it is a savings scheme that pays no interest at all, and that exposes them to the risk that an early recipient will stop contributing once he has been paid. A late member could, it seems, do better by saving the same sums in a bank, and an early member would be the obvious candidate for default.

The usual solutions to the puzzle point to discipline. Saving alone requires a resolve that many people find hard to sustain; a contribution owed to a group that meets every month, whose members will notice and remember a missed payment, supplies that resolve from outside. This is surely part of the answer. But it treats the problem as one between the saver and her own weaker self, whereas members themselves often describe it differently. What makes saving hard, they say, is not temptation so much as other people: the brother who needs money for a wedding, the cousin whose shop has failed, the neighbour whose child is ill. A sum in a bank account is visible to such claims and difficult to refuse. A sum owed to the association is not available, and saying so is an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate.

On this reading the association is not a crude version of a bank but an instrument for managing obligations, one that uses a debt to the group to shelter money from other debts that are harder to decline. The reading also explains why the associations depend so heavily on the density of the ties among their members. The same social pressure that makes a refusal to a cousin acceptable is what keeps the early recipient paying; where members can move away without consequence, or barely know one another, the associations break down, and stories of a member who vanished with the pot are common enough to show that the risk is not imaginary.

None of this implies that formal finance has nothing to offer the people who join such groups, or that the associations are always wise; members of bidding versions sometimes accept heavy discounts out of desperation, and the losses from a collapse can be severe. The point is narrower and, I think, more instructive. The rotating association survives not because its members lack access to something better but because it does something that an ordinary bank account, by design, does not: it makes a sum of money socially unavailable. The question its persistence raises is less why the poor lack banks than what banks, as they are usually designed, lack.

passage: The line-judgement experiments of the 1950s are among the most retold stories in psychology, and the moral usually drawn from them is a gloomy one. A participant sits among strangers who, one after another, give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a standard; when the participant's turn comes, he often repeats their error. The lesson, we are told, is that ordinary people will deny the evidence of their own eyes rather than stand apart from a crowd. This reading has become so familiar that it is easy to forget how much interpretation it smuggles in.

Begin with the numbers that the gloomy version tends to leave out. On the critical trials, most of the answers participants gave were correct, and a sizeable share of people never yielded at all. A study that is remembered as a demonstration of conformity could as easily be remembered as a demonstration of independence under strange and uncomfortable conditions. Which of these stories gets told says more about the teller than about the data.

More important is the question of what yielding meant. Outside the laboratory, when several people who seem competent and sincere all report the same thing, the rational response is to give their reports considerable weight, even against one's own impression. Our senses err, and other people are among the best instruments we have for catching their errors. A participant who reasoned, 'I cannot see why they are all saying this, but it is unlikely that every one of them is mistaken,' was not abandoning reason; he was applying a rule that serves well almost everywhere except in a room deliberately arranged to defeat it. On this view much of what looks like spineless deference is better described as informational influence: treating others as evidence.

None of this means that the pressure in the room was imaginary. Variations in which participants wrote their answers privately, rather than announcing them aloud, produced far less agreement with the majority, which suggests that some yielding was about avoiding embarrassment rather than about belief. Participants interviewed afterwards also described acute discomfort, and some admitted that they had answered against what they saw. Normative pressure, the wish to fit in, was real. The point is not that it was absent but that it was only part of the picture, and that collapsing everything into it produces a caricature.

The caricature matters because it shapes the remedies we prescribe. If people conform because they are weak, the cure is to exhort them to be brave. If they conform partly because they are sensibly using others as sources of information, the cure is better information: making dissent visible, so that a single honest voice breaks the appearance of unanimity, and designing institutions in which the reasons behind a majority view can be inspected rather than merely counted.

passage: Every few generations someone tries to rescue a dying craft by writing it down. A retiring stonemason or bell founder is interviewed at length, his methods are photographed and measured, and the results are published as a manual that, it is hoped, will allow the craft to survive its last practitioners. The manuals are often admirable documents, careful, accurate and lovingly illustrated. They are also, as anyone who has tried to learn from one discovers, strangely inert: the reader can follow every step and still produce work that a practitioner would reject at a glance.

The reason is that much of what a skilled worker knows is not a set of steps at all but a way of perceiving. A smith judges the heat of iron by its colour, and the relevant differences of colour are ones that a novice literally does not see; a joiner hears in the note of a mallet whether a joint has seated; a plasterer feels through the trowel the moment at which the mix has begun to stiffen. Such judgements can be described, but the description presupposes the perception it describes. An instruction to work the metal when it turns the colour of straw is useful only to someone who already knows which straw, in which light, and how much variation is allowed.

Apprenticeship solved this problem not by explaining more but by arranging for the learner to perceive under guidance. The apprentice stood beside the master for years and was told 'now' and 'not yet' thousands of times, until he slowly came to see what the master saw. The words mattered, but chiefly as pointers to experiences the learner was having at that very moment. What passed from one generation to the next was less a body of information than a trained attention.

It would be sentimental to conclude that apprenticeship should simply be restored. It was slow, it was often exploitative, and the guilds that ran it guarded their knowledge as much to keep out competitors as to preserve standards. Nor are manuals useless: to a learner who has already begun to see, a good written account can organise and extend what practice has started. The lesson is narrower. A craft cannot be stored in a text in the way a recipe can, because what has to be preserved is a capacity of persons, and the only reliable way to keep it alive is to keep people practising it alongside others who already can.

passage: The end of empire is usually pictured as a ceremony. A flag is lowered at midnight, another is raised, a governor boards a ship, and a new state takes its seat in the international order. Historians have long known that the picture is too tidy, and a powerful critique, voiced by some of the leaders of newly independent states themselves and given the name neo-colonialism, holds that it is not merely tidy but false. On this account, formal independence changed the personnel and the symbols of rule while leaving its substance intact: the new states still sold raw materials at prices set elsewhere, borrowed from foreign banks, bought foreign manufactures and relied on foreign advisers. The flag changed; the economy did not.

The critique captured something the ceremonial picture ignores, and it remains a useful corrective to triumphal accounts. Yet it shares more with the view it attacks than either side usually admits. Both treat empire as a single thing that either ends or persists, so that the only question is whether the moment of independence marked its end. Empire was not a single thing. It was a bundle of relations, held together by the power of the imperial state: sovereignty over territory and law, control of trade and currency, the organisation of armed force, the training of an administrative and professional class, the language in which public life was conducted, and the habits of deference and aspiration that all these produced. There is no reason to expect such strands to have come apart at the same speed, and they did not.

Sovereignty, the strand that the ceremony marked, ended at a stroke, and its ending was not trivial. A sovereign government could nationalise a foreign-owned mine, change its alliances, write a new constitution, expel a foreign base or make ruinous mistakes of its own, and many did each of these things. Other strands loosened over decades. Monetary arrangements tying several former colonies' currencies to that of the former ruler persisted long after independence; legal systems, curricula and civil-service procedures inherited from the colonial period often outlasted the governments that had installed them; the former metropolis remained, for many, the place where one went to study and to be taken seriously. Some of these continuities were imposed through unequal bargaining at the moment of transfer. Others were chosen, and defended, by new elites who had been formed by the old system and found its institutions congenial.

Seen as an unbundling, decolonisation ceases to be an event that either happened or did not, and becomes a set of processes whose timing differed by strand and by place. This has a practical as well as a historiographical consequence. The question 'When did empire end?' admits no good answer, and debates conducted in its terms tend to stall, with one side pointing to the ceremonies and the other to the trade figures. The better question is which relations were transformed, when, by whom and at what cost. It allows one to say, without contradiction, that a country became fully sovereign in a given year and that its banking system or its universities remained oriented toward its former ruler for a generation.

It also places responsibility more precisely. If the persistence of colonial patterns were simply the continuation of empire by other means, then the governments of independent states would be its passive victims. If some strands were retained by choice, those governments must answer for the choosing, just as former imperial powers must answer for the strands they kept by pressure. The unbundled view is less satisfying than either of the stories it replaces, since it yields no single date and no single villain. That is not a weakness in a historical account; it is usually a sign that the account has begun to fit its subject.

passage: Statements of chance are among the most familiar in science and ordinary life, and among the hardest to interpret. When we say that a fair coin has a chance of one half of landing heads, what are we saying? The most influential answer identifies chance with frequency: the chance of heads is the proportion of heads in a long run of tosses, or the limit towards which that proportion tends as the run is extended without end. The answer has the great merit of tying chance to something that can be counted, and it explains why observed frequencies are our main evidence about chances.

Its difficulties begin with the single case. A particular coin may be tossed once and then melted down; a particular patient either will or will not recover from a particular operation. Yet we speak readily of the chance that this toss lands heads or that this patient recovers, and such judgements guide real decisions. The frequency view can treat them only by placing the single case in a class of similar cases and borrowing the frequency of the class. And here a second difficulty appears, because every case belongs to many classes. The patient is a man of sixty, a non-smoker, a resident of a particular city, someone treated by a particular surgeon, and the recovery rates in these classes may differ considerably. Which frequency is the patient's chance?

Dissatisfaction with this reference class problem has led many to prefer a propensity view, on which chance is a physical tendency of a particular set-up to produce a given outcome, a property the single toss or the single operation possesses whether or not any long run ever occurs. The propensity view handles the single case gracefully, but at a price. It is unclear what a propensity is, beyond a name for whatever it is that frequencies are evidence of, and the view does not escape the problem it was meant to solve. The tendency of a set-up depends on how the set-up is described: the toss described as a toss of a fair coin has one propensity, while the toss described down to the exact force and angle of the flick may have another, close to certainty.

The persistence of the problem across both views suggests that it is not a defect peculiar to either but a feature of chance itself. A chance is not a property an event has simply, but a property it has relative to a specification of the circumstances. Asking for the chance of an event, full stop, is like asking for the speed of a train without saying relative to what: the question is not unanswerable but incomplete. What remains open, and must be settled by our purposes rather than by the world, is which specification to use. For a gambler who cannot measure the flick, the description 'fair coin' is the relevant one; for a physicist with a high-speed camera, it is not.

Some will feel that this concedes too much, making chance a matter of perspective rather than a feature of the world. But relativity to a description is not the same as subjectivity. Once the specification is fixed, the chance is fixed too, and two observers who adopt the same description and disagree about the chance cannot both be right. Velocity is no less objective for being relative to a frame. What the account gives up is only the idea that there is a single privileged description, the one nature itself would choose, and it is far from clear that anything in science requires such a description.

passage: The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection.

The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist.

Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly.

If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first.

The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.

passage: Few findings in happiness research have travelled further than the idea of hedonic adaptation. People who experience a good or bad change in their circumstances, the finding goes, tend over time to drift back towards their earlier level of wellbeing, as though each of us were tethered to a personal set point from which events can pull us only temporarily. In its popular form the idea has hardened into something like a philosophy: since we adapt to everything, the pursuit of better circumstances is futile, and contentment is a matter of temperament rather than of how one lives. The research, read with any care, gives considerably less support to this conclusion than its popularity would suggest.

To begin with, adaptation is uneven. People appear to adjust quite quickly to many gains, such as a higher salary or a larger house, which soon become the new normal against which further comparisons are made. But some conditions resist adaptation stubbornly. Persistent noise, a long and unpredictable commute and chronic pain seem to remain unpleasant year after year, perhaps because they keep demanding attention and never settle into the background of experience. The lesson is not that circumstances do not matter but that they matter selectively: what we stop noticing stops affecting us, and what keeps intruding does not.

A second problem lies in how the evidence is summarised. Many studies report that, on average, a group's wellbeing returns towards its earlier level some time after an event such as marriage or the loss of a job. An average, however, can conceal very different individual paths. A group in which some people end up much happier and others much less happy can show almost no change overall, and the reassuring flat line then describes almost nobody in it. When researchers have examined individuals rather than averages, they have tended to find that a substantial minority do not return to where they began, which is precisely the information that a headline about set points discards.

None of this means that the original insight was mistaken. People do adapt to a great deal, and the observation usefully corrects the belief that one more purchase or promotion will produce lasting delight. The error lies in the step from 'we adapt to much' to 'nothing we do makes a lasting difference'. That step is no more justified than its opposite, and it carries a practical cost, since it can discourage people from changing the very conditions, the noisy flat or the gruelling journey, that are most likely to keep wearing them down.

passage: One of the first lessons of economics is that money is fungible. A rupee earned is the same as a rupee found, a rupee received as a gift or a rupee won at cards; since each can buy exactly what the others can, a rational person should be indifferent to where a sum came from and should spend it according to a single ranking of needs. This is what makes money so useful. It strips goods of their particular histories and renders them comparable, and it lets a stranger in one town trade with a stranger in another without either needing to know anything about the other's life.

Ordinary households, however, behave as though they had never heard the lesson. Coins for the temple are kept in a separate tin; a grandmother's gift to a newborn goes into a savings account that no one will touch for rent even in a hard month; the money a woman earns from tailoring is spent on her children's schooling, while her husband's wages go to food and the loan; a windfall is spent on a celebration that the same sum, arriving as salary, would never have funded. Money that arrives in one way is marked, set aside and spent in another, as though each sum carried a label that its owners were bound to respect. Nor are such habits confined to poor households; in one form or another they appear in families at every level of income.

The standard response is to call this mental accounting and to treat it as a lapse, a cognitive shortcut that serves people tolerably on the whole but leads them into avoidable errors. The errors are real. A family that keeps savings in a low-interest account reserved for a daughter's wedding while borrowing at a ruinous rate to repair the roof is paying heavily for a distinction that, in purely financial terms, does not exist. Yet to describe earmarking only as a mistake is to miss what it accomplishes. The grandmother's gift is set apart because it is a relationship as much as a sum: spending it on rent would feel like dissolving the bond it expressed. The tailor's earnings are spent on schooling because keeping them distinct allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her. Labels on money are the means by which people make it say something about who they are to one another.

It may be objected that this shows only that people attach feelings to money, not that money itself ceases to be fungible. In the market, after all, the tailor's rupee buys exactly what her husband's does, and no shopkeeper asks about its origin. The objection is correct about the shopkeeper. But it concedes the point that matters. Fungibility holds where people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums, as in impersonal trade, and fails where they have not, as in the household, the family ceremony and the circle of friends who lend to one another.

The single, featureless money of the textbook, then, is not a natural property of currency that social life afterwards distorts. It is an arrangement that holds in certain settings and that people are constantly unmaking elsewhere. To see this is not to deny that the arrangement is valuable, or that families sometimes pay dearly for their labels; it is to recognise that the indifference to origins which economics takes as its starting point is itself a social achievement, and a local one.

passage: Special economic zones are usually defended with a simple argument. Where a country's regulations, infrastructure or courts are too poor to attract investors, it may be impossible to repair them everywhere at once; it is easier to draw a boundary around a small area, supply it with reliable power, quick customs clearance and predictable rules, and invite firms to set up inside. The zone becomes a place where the business environment the country cannot yet afford for itself is provided in miniature. Inside the fence, so the thinking goes, investors will find conditions that would take a generation to create outside it.

The reasoning is persuasive within its limits, and it explains why so many governments have tried the experiment. But it also contains the seed of a common failure. A zone designed to protect investors from the surrounding economy can succeed too well. Firms import their components free of duty, assemble them with local labour and export the finished product, while buying almost nothing from domestic suppliers and teaching them nothing. Export figures rise, and an observer counting shipments would call the zone a triumph. Yet the economy outside the fence may be little changed, apart from the wages paid to workers who commute in, and those wages often reflect the kind of routine assembly that is easiest to move elsewhere when costs rise.

What distinguishes the zones that have mattered is not the generosity of their tax holidays but the degree to which they leak. In the more instructive cases, local firms learned to supply the foreign plants, managers trained inside the zone left to start businesses outside it, and, most important, rules first tried within the boundary were later extended across the country once they had shown that they worked. The zone, on this view, is less an enclave than a laboratory, and a laboratory whose findings never leave the building has failed at its central task, whatever it produces.

It would be naive to conclude that governments should simply abolish the boundary and expect the benefits to spread. The isolation of a zone is often what makes it politically possible in the first place, since it lets reformers try new rules without confronting at once every interest that benefits from the old ones. The point is that isolation should be treated as a starting condition to be outgrown, not as the design itself. A zone that is still, after decades, an island of efficiency in an unchanged sea is evidence less of success than of a reform that stalled.

passage: The quarrel between those who lay down rules for English and those who merely record how it is spoken is usually staged as a contest between snobbery and science. On one side stand the guardians of usage, who object to split infinitives and sentence-final prepositions and who regard each new sense of an old word as a small act of vandalism. On the other stand the linguists, who point out that many of the rules are of recent and dubious origin, that admired writers have broken them for centuries, and that a grammar describing what speakers actually do is the only kind that deserves the name. Put this way, the linguists win easily, and in the universities, at least, they have been winning for a long time.

Yet the victory is less complete than it appears, because it rests on a confusion about what a rule of usage is. The linguist is right that no rule of this kind is a law of the language in the way that, say, the order of article and noun is: speakers who break it are still perfectly understood, and they are still speaking English. But it does not follow that such rules are mere prejudice. Beliefs about correctness are themselves part of the linguistic behaviour of a community. A speaker who avoids a construction in a job application while using it freely at home is not confused; she is responding accurately to a social fact, namely that certain readers will judge her by it. A descriptive grammar that ignored such judgements would be describing an imaginary community.

What the prescriptivist gets wrong is not the existence of the rules but their source. The traditional defence appeals to logic, or to the example of Latin, or to a clarity the condemned construction supposedly lacks. These appeals rarely survive inspection. The objection to splitting an infinitive, for instance, makes some sense in a language where the infinitive is a single word and cannot be split, and very little in one where it is two. The real authority of such a rule is conventional: it binds because enough educated readers expect it to be observed, and for no deeper reason.

Seeing the rules as conventions of a register, rather than as laws or as prejudices, changes the question we should ask about them. It is no longer whether a usage is correct in some absolute sense, but whether a given convention earns its keep: whether it marks a distinction readers find useful, or merely sets a test that excludes those who were never taught it. Some conventions pass that test; many fail it. The point is that they can be judged, and that judging them is neither the snob's work nor the scientist's alone.

passage: Few words in urban debate do as much damage as 'density', largely because it is used, often by the same speaker within a single argument, to mean two quite different things. In its technical sense density is a ratio: the number of people, or of dwellings, on a given area of land. In ordinary speech it usually means something closer to crowding, the experience of too many people in too little room: a family of six in a single room, a queue that spills into the road, a train in which nobody can turn round. The two can occur together, but they need not, and treating them as one has shaped a century of planning.

Consider two districts with the same number of residents per hectare. In the first, people live in tall apartment buildings with generous flats, set among parks and wide streets. In the second, the same population is packed into low houses, several households to a building, with lanes too narrow for a cart. On a map of density the districts are identical; to anyone who lives in them they could hardly be more different. Conversely, a scattered agricultural village, where extended families share a single dwelling, can be acutely crowded indoors while being nearly empty by the hectare. Density, in short, describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life.

The confusion has a history. The diseases that ravaged industrial cities in the nineteenth century were widely blamed on density, and reformers responded by trying to spread people out. Yet what made those cities so lethal was a combination of overcrowded rooms, contaminated water and absent sewers, and where water and drains were improved, death rates in dense districts fell even though the districts often remained dense. The reformers were right that something was wrong; they were imprecise about what it was, and the imprecision outlived them, surviving in zoning codes and building regulations long after the sanitary conditions that had justified it had disappeared.

This is not to say that density is costless. Many people living close together compete for parks, school places and quiet, and a district can feel oppressive even when no room in it is overcrowded. Perception counts, and planners who dismiss it will find their schemes resented. But the remedies differ. Crowding is relieved by more floor space per person and by services; the costs of density are managed by design, by open space and by the quality of the street. A policy that caps density in the name of relieving crowding may achieve neither, pushing people into fewer and more crowded rooms, or out to the edge of the city.

passage: Students meeting physics for the first time are often unsettled to learn that the planes in their textbooks have no friction, the pendulums swing without air, and the planets are treated as points. Economics and population biology are worse offenders: their agents calculate perfectly and their populations are infinitely large. A natural response is to say that science, at least in its models, trades truth for convenience, and that a model is a useful fiction whose only virtue is that it lets us calculate. On this view the idealisation is a debt to be repaid later, when better methods allow the missing details to be added back.

This response gets the matter backwards. An idealisation is not usually a lapse in description but a claim about relevance. To leave friction out of an account of a stone sliding down a smooth slope is to assert, implicitly, that friction makes no appreciable difference to the feature one is trying to explain, namely the way the stone's speed grows with time. If that assertion is correct, the idealised model is not a fiction about the stone; it is a true statement about what the stone's motion depends on. The model is false about the world in its details and accurate about the structure of dependence, and the second is frequently what we wanted to know. Adding every missing factor would not improve such a model; it would bury the very pattern the model was built to display.

This does not mean that every idealisation is innocent. The claim of irrelevance can be wrong, and it is often wrong in a particular way: an assumption that holds well within one range of conditions fails outside it. Treating air as absent is harmless for a stone dropped from a window and disastrous for a feather, or for a parachutist. The danger lies less in the falsehood itself than in forgetting that it was a bet about relevance, so that a model calibrated in one setting is carried into another where the bet no longer pays.

The sensible test, then, is not whether a model is literally true, since almost none are, but whether its conclusions survive when the idealisation is relaxed. If a result about a population holds whether the population is taken to be infinite or merely very large, the assumption of infinity was doing no harm. If the result vanishes as soon as the assumption is loosened, it was an artefact of the simplification rather than a discovery about the world. Read in this way, the frictionless plane is less an embarrassment than a hypothesis, and like any hypothesis it can be checked.

passage: It is often said that a scientific theory can never be proved but can always be refuted: no number of successful predictions establishes it, while a single failed one brings it down. The slogan captures something real about the asymmetry between confirmation and refutation, but as a description of how theories should be treated it is too simple. A prediction is never derived from a theory alone. It depends also on assumptions about the instruments used, the conditions of the experiment and the other bodies or forces that might be at work. When a prediction fails, logic tells us that something in this whole bundle is wrong; it does not tell us which part.

The history of astronomy offers a well-known illustration. In the first half of the nineteenth century, the observed orbit of Uranus departed from what Newtonian mechanics predicted. Astronomers did not abandon Newton. They supposed instead that an unseen planet was pulling on Uranus, calculated where it would have to be, and in 1846 Neptune was found close to the predicted position. The anomaly, far from refuting the theory, became one of its most celebrated successes.

The same strategy, however, does not always succeed. A small discrepancy in the orbit of Mercury was also attributed to an undiscovered planet, which some astronomers even named, but no such planet was ever found. The discrepancy was finally accounted for only by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which replaced Newton's account of gravitation rather than adding to it. In hindsight, the two anomalies look entirely different. At the time, they looked much the same, and the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable.

The lesson is not that anomalies should be ignored, nor that theories should be given up at the first sign of trouble. It is that there is no rule which tells us in advance when an anomaly is a puzzle to be solved within a theory and when it is a sign that the theory is failing. Tenacity is a virtue in science, since a theory abandoned at the first difficulty would never have the chance to show what it can do; but tenacity shades into dogma when a theory is protected by one convenient assumption after another, each invented for no reason except to save it. Telling the two apart is a matter of judgement, informed by how many anomalies have accumulated and by whether the assumptions used to explain them away have earned independent support.

passage: It is natural to think of understanding as knowledge in a higher concentration. On this view, a person who understands why bridges stand or why prices rise simply knows more than one who does not: more facts, and in particular more facts about causes. Understanding would then be knowledge of a special subject matter, the reasons why, but it would be knowledge all the same, answerable to the same standards and vulnerable to the same defeats.

The view has difficulty with a familiar figure, the student who has memorised the correct explanation. Asked why the seasons change, she replies, accurately, that the earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit, so that each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for part of the year. She has the answer from a reliable textbook and a reliable teacher, and by most accounts of knowledge she knows why the seasons change. Yet ask her what would happen if the tilt were greater, or why the seasons are reversed between the hemispheres, and she is at a loss. She possesses the explanation as a sentence rather than as something she can use. What she lacks is not a further fact but a grasp of how the facts she already has depend on one another, the ability to follow the explanation into cases for which it was not stated.

If this is right, understanding is less a matter of what one has been told than of what one can do with it, and this has a surprising consequence. Knowledge is usually held to require truth: one cannot know what is false. Understanding seems more forgiving. Much of what we rightly call scientific understanding is achieved through models that are, taken literally, false. The simple model of a gas treats its molecules as points that occupy no space and exert no forces on one another except in collision, which no actual molecule does; yet a student who has mastered that model understands a great deal about why gases behave as they do, and understands it partly because the model leaves out complications that would obscure the pattern. It would be odd to say that her understanding is defective merely because the model is false, and odder still to say that someone who had memorised a more accurate description, but could do nothing with it, understood more.

This should not be taken to mean that understanding floats free of truth altogether. An idealisation earns its place only when its departures from reality are irrelevant to the questions it is used to answer; the point-particle model serves well for gases at ordinary densities and misleads at very high ones, and part of understanding the model is knowing where it stops working. A story that got the dependencies wrong, however fluently it could be manipulated, would yield not understanding but a skilful illusion of it. The claim, then, is not that falsehood is harmless but that the relation between understanding and truth is looser and more selective than the relation between knowledge and truth: understanding demands accuracy in the respects that bear on the dependencies grasped, and tolerates distortion elsewhere.

The distinction matters beyond philosophy. Educational systems that measure success by the reproduction of correct statements will reward the memorising student and may never detect what she is missing, since what she is missing shows itself only when the question changes. Testing for understanding requires, at least in part, asking questions the student has not been prepared for.
